chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

My father wrote in his bequest that I should enshroud him in three garments: one of them is a cloak of his which he used to pray in on Friday, and another garment, and a shirt. So I said to my father, 'Why do you write this?' He said, 'I fear that the people might overpower you, and if they say, 'Enshroud him in four or five,' do not do it. And wrap me with a turban, and do not count the turban as part of the enshrouding; rather, what is counted is what the body is wrapped with.'

key_terms.يُلَفُّ بِهِ الْجَسَدُ: What the body is wrapped with

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on the number of garments for enshrouding the deceased and how is the turban treated?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* highlights the Imams' emphasis on adhering strictly to the Sunnah to prevent *bid'ah* (innovation) through popular custom, specifically limiting the shroud to three pieces as a practical safeguard against social pressure. It clarifies the juristic distinction between items that wrap the body versus those merely worn on the head, a nuance critical in Shia fiqh for determining the minimum obligatory shroud. This instruction reflects the broader Shia principle of simplicity in death rituals while maintaining dignity, rooted in the Prophet's practice.
